patches.old: students may incorrectly add the absolute values without accounting for the sign of the anode, arriving at 2.03 V by subtracting magnitudes instead of applying the correct formula
patches.new: students may subtract the magnitudes, 2.37 − 0.34, instead of subtracting the signed anode potential from the signed cathode potential
patches.reason: The sentence described the error as adding the absolute values and then, in the same breath, as subtracting magnitudes — two different mistakes, and only the second one produces the 2.03 V distractor it is explaining. Adding the absolute values would give the correct 2.71 V.

visual.title: The galvanic cell, and which way everything moves
visual.alt: A zinc-copper galvanic cell. On the left a zinc electrode stands in zinc ion solution, labelled anode, negative, oxidation, losing mass, with the half-reaction Zn to Zn2+ plus two electrons. On the right a copper electrode stands in copper ion solution, labelled cathode, positive, reduction, gaining mass, with Cu2+ plus two electrons to Cu. A wire across the top carries electrons from left to right through a voltmeter reading 1.10 volts. A salt bridge of potassium nitrate joins the two beakers, with nitrate migrating left into the anode compartment and potassium right into the cathode compartment. A panel below gives the cell notation and the formula E cell equals cathode minus anode worked out as 0.34 minus minus 0.76 equals plus 1.10 volts.
visual.caption: Two circuits, not one: electrons through the wire from anode to cathode, ions through the salt bridge in the opposite sense to keep each beaker neutral.
